Definition: Steadfast love, mercy and loyal covenant kindness — God's unfailing commitment to His people that never depends on their worthiness.
BiblicalUsage: Hesed appears over 250 times, most often of God. The Psalms repeat it in refrain — 'His steadfast love endures forever' — and the prophets call Israel to practice hesed toward others, not just feel it.
TheologicalSignificance: Hesed is the love that will not let go. It assures believers that God's kindness is covenant loyalty, not mood — a firm anchor when feelings and circumstances shift.
RelatedTopics: Grace; Mercy; Covenant; Love of God

Definition: Peace, wholeness and complete well-being — not merely the absence of conflict but life flourishing as God intended.
BiblicalUsage: Shalom describes health, prosperity, right relationships and rest. Priests blessed Israel with it, prophets promised it under the coming Prince of Peace, and Isaiah tied it to the suffering Servant who was punished to bring us peace.
TheologicalSignificance: Shalom shows salvation is wholeness, not just rescue. In Christ, the God of peace restores what sin fractured — our hearts, our relationships and one day all creation.

Definition: A covenant — a solemn, binding promise and relationship, often sealed with sacrifice, signs and blessings and curses.
BiblicalUsage: Berit structures the whole Bible story: covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel, David and finally the new covenant in Christ. Each one is initiated by God's grace and calls for a faithful response.
TheologicalSignificance: Because God binds Himself by covenant, hope rests on His promise, not our performance. Berit is why believers can trust that God will finish what He began.

Definition: Faithfulness, steadfastness and firm trustworthiness; by extension, the steady faith that trusts and obeys God.
BiblicalUsage: Emunah most often describes God Himself — 'the Rock, His work is perfect... a God of faithfulness.' Habakkuk's 'the righteous shall live by his faith' became a cornerstone text quoted by Paul.
TheologicalSignificance: Emunah reminds us faith is not a leap in the dark but trust in a God who is utterly steady. Our faith rests on His faithfulness first.

Definition: Instruction, teaching and law — God's gracious direction for life, centred in the books of Moses but embracing all His revealed guidance.
BiblicalUsage: Torah is broader than rules: it is a Father's instruction to be loved, meditated on day and night and taught to children. The Psalms delight in it rather than merely enduring it.
TheologicalSignificance: Torah reframes God's commands as a gift, not a burden. For Christians, Christ fulfils the Torah and the Spirit writes its heart on us, guiding us in grateful obedience.

Definition: Spirit, breath and wind — the life-giving presence and power of God, and the breath that animates every living creature.
BiblicalUsage: Ruach hovers over creation, breathes life into Adam, fills prophets and craftsmen, and in Ezekiel raises dry bones to life. Its range — wind, breath, Spirit — shows one powerful, personal presence at work.
TheologicalSignificance: Ruach is hope for the lifeless places: the same Spirit who raised dry bones in Ezekiel and raised Jesus from the dead lives in believers, renewing what seemed beyond repair.

Definition: Soul, life, self or living being — the whole person as a living, desiring, God-breathed creature.
BiblicalUsage: Nephesh does not mean a detachable ghost inside the body; Adam 'became a living nephesh.' The Psalms speak of the nephesh thirsting for God, blessing the Lord and finding rest in Him alone.
TheologicalSignificance: Nephesh teaches that God cares for the whole person — body, mind, longings and life itself. The soul that thirsts for God finds its anchor and satisfaction in Him.

Definition: Holy, set apart and sacred — describing God's utter distinctness and purity, and people or things consecrated to Him.
BiblicalUsage: Seraphim cry 'Holy, holy, holy' before God's throne, and Israel is called to be holy because God is holy. Qadosh marks what belongs to God and must be treated with reverence and purity.
TheologicalSignificance: God's holiness is not distant coldness — the Holy One of Israel draws near to redeem. His call 'be holy, for I am holy' is an invitation into His own character.

Definition: Righteousness and justice — rightness measured by God's character, expressed in fair dealing, integrity and setting things right.
BiblicalUsage: Tsedeq and its family of words describe God's reign founded on righteousness and justice. The prophets longed for justice to 'roll down like waters' in a land that had abandoned God's standard.
TheologicalSignificance: Tsedeq assures a hurting world that God sees injustice and will set things right. In Christ, God's righteousness is both revealed and gifted to all who believe.

Definition: Love — deep affection, devotion and delight, used of God's love for His people and of human love in marriage, family and friendship.
KeyPassages: Deuteronomy 6:5; Song of Solomon 8:7; Jeremiah 31:3; Zephaniah 3:17
BiblicalUsage: Ahavah commands our whole-hearted love for God in the Shema and celebrates love 'strong as death' in the Song of Solomon. Jeremiah hears God say, 'I have loved you with an everlasting love.'
TheologicalSignificance: Ahavah shows love in Scripture is covenant devotion, not passing feeling. God's everlasting ahavah is the root from which all our loving grows.

Definition: To know — not merely to hold facts but to know by experience, intimacy and covenant relationship.
BiblicalUsage: Yada describes Adam knowing Eve, God knowing Abraham, and the new covenant promise that all 'shall know the Lord.' God desires experiential knowledge of Him more than empty sacrifice.
TheologicalSignificance: Yada is a comfort and an invitation: we are fully known by God, and eternal life is growing to know Him truly — knowledge that is relationship, not just information.
RelatedTopics: Knowledge of God; Covenant; Eternal Life

Definition: To return, turn back and repent — turning away from sin and returning home to God.
BiblicalUsage: Shuv is the prophets' great call: 'Return to the Lord your God, for you have stumbled.' It pictures repentance as a homecoming journey, and God promises that when Israel returns, He restores.
TheologicalSignificance: Shuv means no one has wandered too far to come home. Repentance is not grovelling — it is turning toward a Father who says, 'Return to Me, and I will return to you.'

Definition: To wait for, hope in and expect — the tense, trusting waiting of a watchman or a taut cord stretched in anticipation.
BiblicalUsage: Those who kavah — who wait for the Lord — 'shall renew their strength' and mount up like eagles. The word's link to a stretched cord captures hope under tension that does not snap.
TheologicalSignificance: Kavah dignifies waiting: biblical hope is not wishful thinking but strong, expectant trust. The cord holds because the One we wait for is faithful.

Definition: Redeemer or kinsman-redeemer — the near relative who buys back family land, freedom or honour for one who cannot rescue themselves.
BiblicalUsage: Boaz as goel redeems Ruth and Naomi's future, and Job cries out, 'I know that my Redeemer lives.' Isaiah applies the title to the Lord Himself, Israel's Redeemer and Holy One.
TheologicalSignificance: Goel makes redemption personal and familial: God is not a distant rescuer but a near kinsman who pays the price Himself. Job's hope — and ours — rests on a living Redeemer.

Definition: A musical and liturgical marker in the Psalms, likely signalling a pause to reflect, lift up the voice, or let the truth settle.
BiblicalUsage: Selah appears 71 times in the Psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3, always after a weighty statement about God. Whatever its exact musical meaning, it creates space to stop and consider.
TheologicalSignificance: Selah teaches the rhythm of hope: pause, breathe and ponder who God is before rushing on. Reflection turns true words into anchored convictions.

Definition: Word, speech, matter or thing — God's spoken word that creates, commands, promises and always accomplishes His purpose.
BiblicalUsage: By the dabar of the Lord the heavens were made, and His word 'shall not return to Me empty.' Israel learned to live not by bread alone but by every word from God's mouth.
TheologicalSignificance: Dabar assures us God's promises are not fragile. The word that created galaxies and sustained Israel still accomplishes everything God sends it to do.
RelatedTopics: Word of God; Promises of God; Creation

Definition: Glory — literally weightiness and substance; God's radiant majesty and honour, and the dignity He shares with His image-bearers.
BiblicalUsage: God's kabod filled the tabernacle so Moses could not enter, and Isaiah heard the whole earth is full of it. To give God glory is to recognise the weight of who He truly is.
TheologicalSignificance: Kabod anchors our worth and our worship: the King of glory is not far away — He fills His creation and invites His people to reflect His glory.

Definition: Justice, judgement and ordinance — God's righteous decisions and the just order He requires in courts, community and daily life.
BiblicalUsage: Mishpat is what God requires — 'to do justice, love kindness and walk humbly' — and what corrupt courts perverted. Kings were judged by whether the poor received mishpat under their reign.
TheologicalSignificance: Mishpat shows faith is never private only: the God of justice calls His people to defend the vulnerable. His final judgement means wrongs will not have the last word.

Definition: Hope — confident expectation of good to come, grounded in God's faithfulness rather than in circumstances or chance.
BiblicalUsage: Unlike everyday Greek usage, where hope could be uncertain, New Testament elpis rests on Christ's resurrection. Peter calls it a 'living hope,' and Paul names its object: 'Christ in you, the hope of glory.'
TheologicalSignificance: Elpis is this blog's heartbeat: 'We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure.' Christian hope is not optimism — it is certainty about God's future, holding us steady today.

Definition: An anchor — the heavy iron hook that holds a ship fast against wind and waves; used figuratively in Hebrews for hope in Christ.
BiblicalUsage: Agkura appears literally in Acts 27, where sailors drop four anchors in a storm, and figuratively in Hebrews 6:19, where hope itself is the anchor — fixed not in shifting seabeds but within the veil, where Jesus has gone.
TheologicalSignificance: Agkura turns a nautical tool into a promise: your soul need not drift. Hope is anchored to Christ Himself, already secure in the heavenly holy place on your behalf.

Definition: Self-giving, sacrificial love that seeks the highest good of the other — the love God is, shows in Christ, and pours into His people.
BiblicalUsage: Agape was a fairly ordinary Greek word until the New Testament filled it with cross-shaped meaning. God 'is agape,' demonstrated it while we were still sinners, and commands it as the mark of His people.
TheologicalSignificance: Agape is love that acts, gives and stays. Because God loved us first at such cost, our love for others can be patient, kind and unafraid.

Definition: Grace — God's free, unmerited favour and gift, and the power His favour gives for living and serving.
BiblicalUsage: Charis was the language of gift and thankfulness that Paul transformed into the gospel's signature word: saved 'by grace... through faith... not by works.' Grace upon grace flows from Christ's fullness.
TheologicalSignificance: Charis means your standing with God is gift from start to finish — and when you are weak, that grace is not only pardon but strength: 'My grace is sufficient for you.'

Definition: Faith — trust, belief and faithfulness; active reliance on God and His promises, expressed in allegiance and obedience.
BiblicalUsage: Pistis can mean both our trust in God and faithfulness itself — Hebrews 11 parades men and women whose faith acted, endured and obeyed. Paul insists the righteous live by pistis from first to last.
TheologicalSignificance: Pistis is not believing in spite of evidence but trusting a trustworthy Person. Faith is the hand that receives grace and the feet that keep walking with God.

Definition: Word, message, reason and account — God's self-expression, culminating in Jesus Christ, the Word made flesh.
BiblicalUsage: Logos carried rich meaning for Jews (God's creative word) and Greeks (the reason ordering the universe). John seizes both: the Logos was God, was with God, and became flesh in Jesus.
TheologicalSignificance: Logos declares that God has spoken — finally and personally — in His Son. We do not guess at God's heart; we look at Jesus, the Word made flesh.
RelatedTopics: Jesus Christ; Word of God; Incarnation

Definition: Spirit, breath and wind — the Holy Spirit, the third Person of the Trinity, and the unseen dimension of human life.
BiblicalUsage: Pneuma echoes Hebrew ruach: the wind blows where it wishes, the Spirit fell at Pentecost with a sound like rushing wind, and He now intercedes, indwells and bears fruit in believers.
TheologicalSignificance: Pneuma means believers are never left to manage the Christian life alone. The Spirit who raised Jesus lives in us — helper, seal and guarantee of what is coming.

Definition: Church — the assembly or congregation of God's called-out people, gathered locally and universal across all time and place.
BiblicalUsage: Ekklesia was a civic word for a summoned assembly that Scripture claims for God's people. Jesus promises to build His ekklesia, and not even the gates of Hades will overcome it.
TheologicalSignificance: Ekklesia reminds lonely believers they belong to something Christ is building and loves — a people He gave Himself for, secure across every century and storm.

Definition: Salvation, deliverance and preservation — God's rescue of His people from sin, death and judgement into life and wholeness.
BiblicalUsage: Soteria echoes Exodus rescue language and fills it out in Christ: salvation has come to Zacchaeus's house, and there is salvation in no one else. It spans past rescue, present working-out and future completion.
TheologicalSignificance: Soteria is comprehensive rescue — forgiven, being transformed, and certain of glory. The God who began salvation will complete it, which is why hope does not disappoint.

Definition: Righteousness and justice — God's right character and saving action, and the righteous standing He gives to those in Christ.
BiblicalUsage: Dikaiosyne was the word that gripped Martin Luther: in the gospel a righteousness from God is revealed, received by faith. Jesus calls hungering for it blessed and promises it will be filled.
TheologicalSignificance: Dikaiosyne is gospel gold: God is righteous, and in Christ He makes sinners righteous — counted right with God and being made right in daily life.

Definition: Repentance — a change of mind and heart that turns the whole person from sin to God.
BiblicalUsage: Metanoia literally means a mind transformed. John the Baptist and Jesus both opened their preaching with it, and heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents — godly grief produces a repentance leading to life.
TheologicalSignificance: Metanoia is good news, not bad: turning is possible because God is near and kind. Repentance is not paying for pardon — it is the doorway into joy.

Definition: Fellowship, partnership and sharing — the deep common life believers share with God and one another, expressed in generosity.
BiblicalUsage: The first church devoted itself to koinonia — shared meals, shared possessions, shared mission. Paul uses it for partnership in the gospel and for our fellowship with the Father and His Son.
TheologicalSignificance: Koinonia says faith was never meant to be solitary. We share life with the Trinity and with one another — an anchored community in a drifting world.

Definition: Peace — harmony, well-being and reconciliation with God, translating the wholeness of Hebrew shalom into the New Testament.
BiblicalUsage: Eirene flows from justification: 'having been justified by faith, we have peace with God.' Christ Himself 'is our peace,' leaving His own peace with His disciples on the night before the cross.
TheologicalSignificance: Eirene is not the world's fragile calm. It is Christ's own peace guarding hearts and minds — peace with God that becomes the peace of God.

Definition: Glory, honour and radiance — God's manifest splendour, the praise due to Him, and the future glory awaiting His people.
BiblicalUsage: Doxa translates Hebrew kabod. Angels announced it at Bethlehem, Jesus displayed it in signs and transfiguration, and Paul insists present sufferings cannot compare with the doxa to be revealed.
TheologicalSignificance: Doxa gives suffering a horizon: an eternal weight of glory is being prepared that will make today's heaviest trials look light by comparison.

Definition: Sin — missing the mark; rebellion, guilt and the corrupted condition that separates humanity from God and fractures everything else.
BiblicalUsage: Hamartia names sin as both acts we commit and a power that enslaves. All have sinned and fall short of God's glory — yet John announces the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
TheologicalSignificance: Naming hamartia honestly is the first step to hope: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive. The diagnosis is grave precisely because the cure is glorious.

Definition: Gospel — the good news, originally an announcement of victory or a king's arrival, claimed by the church for Jesus Christ.
BiblicalUsage: Euangelion was imperial language — news of Caesar's victories — repurposed for a crucified King. Mark opens 'the gospel of Jesus Christ,' and Paul is not ashamed of it, for it is God's power for salvation.
TheologicalSignificance: Euangelion is announcement before it is advice: something has happened — Christ died, is risen and reigns. Hope rests on news, not on our efforts to be newsworthy.

Definition: Lord, master and sir — the title used for God in the Greek Old Testament and confessed of Jesus as divine Lord.
BiblicalUsage: Kurios renders God's covenant name in the Septuagint, so calling Jesus kurios is explosive: 'Jesus is Lord' is the church's first creed, and every tongue will one day confess it.
TheologicalSignificance: Kurios settles the question of who is in charge — and it is good news. The Lord who anchors our hope is Jesus, exalted, reigning and returning.

Definition: Christ, Messiah, Anointed One — the promised King and deliverer anointed by the Spirit, fulfilled in Jesus of Nazareth.
BiblicalUsage: Christos translates Hebrew Mashiach. Kings, priests and prophets were anointed; Jesus is the Anointed One in whom all three offices meet, confessed by Peter: 'You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.'
TheologicalSignificance: Christos means our hope has a name and a throne. Jesus is not merely a teacher who points the way — He is God's promised King, anointed to save His people.

Definition: Baptism — immersion or washing in water signifying union with Christ in His death and resurrection, repentance and new life.
BiblicalUsage: Baptisma pictures a burial and a rising: baptised into Christ's death, raised to walk in newness of life. It is the public sign of the washing and union God works through the gospel.
TheologicalSignificance: Baptisma gives believers a moment to point back to: I have been buried and raised with Christ. When assurance wavers, baptism preaches the gospel back to us.

Definition: Witness — one who testifies to what they have seen and heard, even at great cost; the root of the English word martyr.
BiblicalUsage: Martys begins as courtroom language: witnesses testify to facts. Because so many Christian witnesses sealed their testimony with their lives — like Antipas in Revelation — the word came to mean martyr.
TheologicalSignificance: Martys dignifies ordinary testimony: you are Christ's witness where you live. And we run surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses who prove God keeps His people.

Definition: Helper, Advocate, Comforter and Counsellor — one called alongside to help; Jesus's title for the Holy Spirit, and for Himself.
BiblicalUsage: Parakletos is courtroom and family language together: an advocate who speaks for you and a helper who stands beside you. Jesus promises 'another Parakletos' — the Spirit — because He Himself is our advocate with the Father.
TheologicalSignificance: Parakletos means you never face trial, grief or accusation alone. Heaven has stationed an Advocate beside you forever — that is anchored hope for anxious hearts.

Definition: Truth — reality as it truly is, God's faithfulness and reliability, embodied and spoken by Jesus Christ.
BiblicalUsage: Aletheia in Greek thought meant unconcealed reality. Jesus claims not merely to teach it but to be it — 'I am the way, and the truth, and the life' — and promises the truth will set people free.
TheologicalSignificance: Aletheia assures a confused age that truth is not a weapon or a trend but a Person who can be known and trusted. His word is truth, and it sanctifies.
RelatedTopics: Truth; Jesus Christ; Word of God

Definition: Life — full, eternal, God-given life, as distinct from mere biological existence; the life Jesus came to give abundantly.
BiblicalUsage: John uses zoe nearly fifty times: eternal life is knowing God, having the Son, and drinking living water now — not only living forever but truly living, starting today.
TheologicalSignificance: Zoe means Christianity is not mere survival or fire insurance. Christ gives life with a capital L — abundant now and unending forever.

Definition: Death — physical death and the spiritual separation from God that sin brings, ultimately defeated by Christ's resurrection.
BiblicalUsage: Thanatos enters through sin and reigns over humanity — until Easter. Paul taunts it directly: 'O death, where is your victory?' Revelation promises a day when death shall be no more.
TheologicalSignificance: Thanatos has met its match. Because Christ died and rose, death is a defeated enemy and a doorway, not a terminus — the anchor holds on the far side of the grave.

Definition: Way, road and journey — a path of life; the earliest name for the Christian faith, and Jesus's own claim about Himself.
BiblicalUsage: Before they were called Christians, believers were followers of 'the Way' (hodos). Jesus declares He is the Way — not one route among many but the road home to the Father Himself.
TheologicalSignificance: Hodos pictures faith as a journey with a sure direction. However winding your road feels, Jesus is both the path and the destination — you cannot lose your way while you stay with Him.

Definition: Light — physical light and, figuratively, truth, purity and life; used of God, of Christ as Light of the world, and of His people.
BiblicalUsage: Phos opens John's Gospel: the life was the light of men, and the darkness has not overcome it. Jesus claims the title, then astonishingly gives it to His followers: 'You are the light of the world.'
TheologicalSignificance: Phos is hope with a guarantee: darkness never wins. The Light has come, still shines, and now shines through ordinary people in ordinary places.

Definition: Darkness — physical darkness and, figuratively, ignorance, evil and separation from the light of God.
BiblicalUsage: Skotia describes the realm people love instead of the light — yet it is a realm God rescues us from, transferring us into His Son's kingdom. John insists the darkness is passing away because the true light is already shining.
TheologicalSignificance: Skotia is real, but it is retreating. No darkness in your story is permanent for those in Christ: He came so that no one who believes need stay in the dark.

Definition: Holy, sacred and set apart — describing God, the Holy Spirit, and believers called saints, consecrated to God.
BiblicalUsage: Hagios is the New Testament's everyday word for Christians: 'saints' — holy ones — not because of their record but because of their position in Christ. Heaven's cry remains 'Holy, holy, holy.'
TheologicalSignificance: Hagios gives ordinary believers an honoured identity: set apart, beloved and being made holy. Who you are in Christ anchors how you live each day.

Definition: Soul, life and inner self — the living person, seat of mind, will and emotion; the Greek counterpart to Hebrew nephesh.
BiblicalUsage: Psuche is what Jesus says can be gained or lost with the whole world at stake — and what He invites to find rest in Him: 'you will find rest for your souls.' It is the precious, eternal core of a person.
TheologicalSignificance: Psuche guards our priorities: nothing profits a person who trades their soul away. In Christ, the soul finds the rest, worth and safekeeping it was made for.

Definition: God — the supreme Creator, ruler and Father; the central word for deity throughout the Greek Scriptures.
BiblicalUsage: Theos appears over 1,300 times in the New Testament. The Bible never argues theos into existence; it announces Him — the God who is for us, who so loved the world, who rewards those who seek Him.
TheologicalSignificance: Theos is the anchor behind the anchor: if God is for us, who can be against us? Every word study in this collection finally points back to Him.

Definition: Flesh — the human body, human nature, and in Paul often humanity in its weakness and rebellion against God, apart from the Spirit.
BiblicalUsage: Sarx spans neutral (the Word became flesh) to deeply negative (the mind set on the flesh). Paul contrasts life kata sarka — according to the flesh — with life according to the Spirit.
TheologicalSignificance: Sarx explains the inner war every believer knows, and why victory is by the Spirit, not willpower. The Word became sarx to redeem sarx — flesh is not beyond His reach.

Definition: Time as appointed season or decisive moment — God's opportune, purposeful timing, distinct from chronos, mere clock time.
BiblicalUsage: Jesus opens His ministry announcing 'the kairos is fulfilled,' and Paul writes that 'when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth His Son.' Kairos moments are history's turning points, timed by heaven.
TheologicalSignificance: Kairos consoles everyone waiting on God: His timing is not delay but design. The God who sent His Son at exactly the right moment can be trusted with your seasons too.
